transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's a bit of a long story, but the main thing, the thing that really made me realize I needed to come in—or at least, what my manager started noticing—is that I just cannot, for the life of me, keep my mind on one single thing anymore. 

I've been working as a software developer for years, and usually I can just lock in, you know? Put the headphones on, get in the zone, and just write code for hours. But lately... it's like my brain is a web browser with a hundred tabs open and they're all playing audio at the same time. I'll be right in the middle of fixing this incredibly complex rendering bug—which is a whole other issue because our legacy codebase is an absolute disaster right now—but I'll be typing, literally right in the middle of a line of code, and a Slack ping will go off. Normally, you just ignore it, right? But for me, it's like this intense physical pull. I jump over to Slack, and then while I'm looking at that, I'll notice the color pattern on my second monitor, like the hex codes are suddenly the most fascinating thing in the world, and I start thinking about color theory and completely redesigning the user interface. 

Or, even worse, a siren will go off outside my window—I live near a pretty busy intersection—and suddenly I'm completely consumed by the noise, thinking about the Doppler effect or mapping out where the fire truck is going, and I've started researching or writing down a whole new idea before I've even finished typing the semicolon on that original line of code. Everything just grabs my attention, every little sound or thought, and I just can't filter any of it out anymore to actually finish what I started.
Are you finding it difficult to meet your work deadlines or fulfill your responsibilities at your job due to these attention issues?

Well, that's... yeah, that's actually the other half of why I'm here. Meeting deadlines isn't even the issue anymore because, well, they actually put me on administrative leave. Which, honestly, I still think is a massive overreaction on their part. See, because I had all these incredible ideas—like I was telling you about the UI redesign and the color theory—I realized our entire deployment pipeline was just sluggish. It was holding us back. So, I figured, why wait for the weekly sprint review? Why wait for three different managers to sign off on something that I *knew* was brilliant? 

So I just... I bypassed the approval protocols. I had the admin privileges, obviously, because I've been there forever, and I just pushed a whole batch of changes straight to production. I mean, I thought I was doing them a favor, streamlining things, you know? But my manager pulled me into a Zoom call the next morning, looking completely panicked, and told me I was a "liability" right now and forced me onto medical leave. Just like that. 

And it’s not just work, honestly. The fallout has been bleeding into my home life, too. My wife, Sarah, she's... she's been incredibly stressed. She sat me down a few days ago—well, it was less of a sit-down and more of a really intense argument in the kitchen—and she told me that between me not working, the money I've been spending on all these new side projects I started, and just how irritable I get when she tries to slow me down... she said the whole house feels completely unstable. Like she’s walking on eggshells around me. And I hate that she feels that way, I really do, but I just feel like she’s not seeing the bigger picture of what I’m trying to accomplish. But yeah, to answer your question, my responsibilities are pretty much out the window right now.
Do you often act on impulse without considering the consequences of your actions?

Well, "without considering the consequences" is a strong way to put it, I think. It's more like... the consequences don't seem as important as the momentum, you know? Like, I told you about pushing that update without approval. I didn't do that just to be reckless. I did it because waiting for another two-week sprint cycle, waiting for the QA team to drag their feet, and then getting a manager to sign off—it just felt like letting the whole opportunity die. The code was right there, it was ready, it was beautiful, honestly, and the idea of letting it sit in a repository gathering dust while some middle manager deliberated over it was physically painful to me. So I pushed it. I knew they wouldn't like it, but I thought the results would speak for themselves. I thought they'd see the metrics improve and thank me. 

And, well, it's the same thing with the projects at home that Sarah is so upset about. I haven't just been sitting around on this leave. I've been building out the infrastructure for this completely new, decentralized application idea I had. And to do that right, you can't just run it on a standard laptop. You need serious processing power. So, yeah, I spent some money we hadn't explicitly agreed on. I bought a stack of high-end GPUs—which, by the way, are incredibly hard to source right now, so I actually had to snipe them from an online auction at like 3 AM, which was a whole adrenaline rush in itself. And then, because I knew this idea was going to be huge, I went ahead and ordered print materials, like really high-quality glossy brochures and business cards, and I even paid a freelancer on Upwork to cut together a couple of promo videos for the launch. 

I mean, to Sarah, it looks like I'm just burning through our savings on a whim. But to me, it's an investment. It's like... if you see a gold mine, you don't wait around to ask for permission to buy a shovel, right? You just buy the shovel and start digging. But I guess, looking back, pushing that code and buying all that gear... it did cause a lot of fallout. I just didn't think the fallout would outweigh the success.
Do you often feel restless or have trouble sitting still?

Restless? Yeah. Yes, absolutely, but... it's not just like tapping my foot or fidgeting, you know? It’s so much bigger than that. It’s more like... I’ve been running on this constant, high-voltage current. It's just buzzing right under my skin all the time. I mean, I'll wake up in the morning, and the second my eyes open—honestly, even before they open—my brain is already going at a million miles an hour. I'm immediately planning out new features for that decentralized app I was telling you about, mapping out the whole architecture in my head. 

And it's not just the code changes, either, because you have to think about the whole ecosystem if you want a project to actually succeed. So I'm barely out of bed, and I'm already planning exhibition layouts for when we launch this thing at major tech conferences, figuring out the press angles, scripting how to pitch it to tech journalists so they see the absolute paradigm shift it represents. 

So, with all of that happening, with all that momentum... how could I possibly just sit around? Sarah will ask me to just sit down at the kitchen table, or try to get me to watch a movie on the couch, and I try, I really do try to appease her, but five minutes in, I'm literally vibrating. Sitting still just feels like... it feels like I'm actively wasting the moment. Every second I'm sitting there doing nothing is a second I could be building, creating, pushing this vision forward. It's almost physically painful to be stationary. I just have to be moving, pacing the hallway, typing up proposals, mapping things out on the whiteboard—doing *something*. If I just sit there, I feel like all that electricity is just going to short-circuit my brain.
Do you often feel extremely happy or euphoric for no apparent reason?

Happy? Euphoric? Well, I wouldn't say it's for *no* apparent reason, because to me, the reason is incredibly obvious. But yes, most days right now, I just feel completely lit up. It’s this profound, overarching sense of being totally unstoppable. I’ll wake up and it’s like the whole world has suddenly snapped into high definition. I look out the window and I just feel this immense, expansive joy, because it finally feels like Glendale caught up with what I've been building all these years. It’s like the whole city, the whole tech ecosystem here, is finally ready for the vision I’ve been trying to push. I'm seeing connections that nobody else is seeing, and realizing that I'm on the verge of something that's going to completely change the landscape... it’s an incredible high. It really is. 

But, and this is the frustrating part, because I'm operating on this entirely different, elevated frequency, it is absolutely excruciating when people try to drag me back down. So while I feel amazing on my own, the second someone gets in my way, I snap. I mean, I snap hard. 

My wife will come into the office while I’m in the absolute zone, trying to get me to pause and talk about a grocery list or some household chore, or my coworkers—well, before the leave, anyway—they’d want to schedule yet another redundant sync-up meeting. And they always use that word. "Process." They want to slow me down with what they call "process." I hear that word and my blood just boils. It feels like they are intentionally throwing sand into the engine of a Formula One car. I just lose my temper completely. I'll yell, I'll get incredibly short with them, because how can they not see that their little administrative hurdles and their need for "process" are literally suffocating brilliance? So it's this weird mix, you know? I'm on top of the world, I've never felt more capable or brilliant in my life, but I am surrounded by people who just want to tie me down with red tape, and it makes me furious.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Sleep? Honestly, sleep just feels... irrelevant right now. I don't know if I'd call it "having trouble" sleeping, because that implies I'm lying in bed, staring at the ceiling, tossing and turning, wishing I could drift off. It’s not like that at all. It’s more like my body and my brain just don't require it anymore. 

I mean, normally, I’d be the guy who needs a solid seven or eight hours, right? I'd have my whole evening routine, maybe read a bit, wind down. But lately? The past couple of weeks? I might lie down for maybe... two hours? Maybe three, if Sarah really gets on my case and insists I come to bed. But even then, I’m just resting my eyes. My mind is still running the calculations, still compiling code in my head, still mapping out the server architecture for the decentralized app. 

And then, boom, it's 3:00 AM, and I am wide awake, completely refreshed, totally energized. I don't feel groggy, I don't need coffee. I just get up and go straight to the whiteboard or the computer. Because why would I waste time unconscious when I have all these breakthroughs happening? Sleep just feels like this outdated biological requirement that I’ve somehow managed to bypass. Sarah keeps telling me I’m going to crash, that it’s not sustainable, but she doesn't understand that I don't *feel* tired. I feel more awake than I have in my entire life. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm having trouble sleeping. I'm just... not really doing it, and I feel fantastic without it.
Do you feel like your current state is causing problems in your relationships or daily life?

Problems? I mean... it depends on who you ask, right? If you ask me, I’m getting more done than I have in the last decade. But if you ask the people around me... yeah, I guess they’d say it’s causing problems. It’s just that they don’t see the big picture. 

Take work, for example. I was telling you about my coworkers and their obsession with "process." Well, last week, I had this absolute breakthrough on the backend architecture. I saw exactly how to optimize the data flow, and it was beautiful. It was elegant. But I knew if I submitted it for review, it would sit in the queue for days, maybe weeks, while they nitpicked every little thing. So I just bypassed the approval protocols and pushed the deployment myself. I mean, why wait when you know you're right? But man, they did not see it that way. My manager called me in, completely ignoring the fact that I had just improved our system efficiency by at least twenty percent, and just went off about protocol and risk. They ended up putting me on mandatory leave. Mandatory leave! They literally benched their best developer because I was moving too fast for them to keep up. So, yeah, I guess technically that’s a "problem," but I see it as them holding me back.

And then there's Sarah. My wife. She... well, she’s been really struggling with all of this. She says things feel incredibly unstable at home right now, and she’s always bringing up the arguments. Like I said before, I have a really short fuse right now when people interrupt me or try to slow me down, and unfortunately, she catches a lot of that. If she asks me to take out the trash while I’m in the middle of writing a proposal, I just explode. I can’t help it. And then there's the money thing. She’s really upset about the spending. I’ve been buying a lot of server equipment—top-of-the-line stuff, because if I’m going to build this decentralized app while I’m on leave, I need the right infrastructure, right? And I might have booked a few non-refundable flights to tech conferences for next year, just to secure my spots. To me, it’s an investment in the future. But to her, she just sees the credit card bills piling up, and she panics. She says she doesn't know who I am right now, which is crazy, because I finally feel like I’m exactly who I was always meant to be. So... yes, it’s causing friction. A lot of friction. But I really believe once this app launches and they see what I’ve been working toward, they’ll understand why I had to push so hard.
How long have you been feeling this way?

How long? Well, if we're tracing it back to the exact inception point... it’s been about three months. Yes, right around three months. That was the exact moment everything shifted, because that’s when my platform was officially selected for the Glendale showcase. 

I don't know if you're familiar with the Glendale showcase, but in my sector, it is the absolute proving ground for emerging tech. I remember exactly where I was when the notification came through. I was actually sitting in one of those incredibly tedious sync-up meetings I told you about, completely zoning out while my manager droned on about Q3 deliverables, and my phone buzzed under the desk. I looked down, and there it was. Acceptance. Validation. 

And honestly, doctor, from that exact second, it was like a switch flipped in my brain. The fog just completely lifted. I realized in an instant that everything I had been building wasn't just some pet project, it was the foundation for an entire ecosystem. So for the last ninety days, it has been this constant, beautiful upward trajectory. Month one was all about conceptualizing the expansion, month two was laying down the new infrastructure—which is why I had to buy all those new servers for the house, obviously—and now, here in month three, I am just executing on a level that is frankly unprecedented. 

So yeah, about three months of this absolute clarity. Sarah acts like this just happened overnight, but it's been a steady, ninety-day ramp-up of pure innovation since that Glendale announcement. It’s just wild to think that all it took was that one committee finally recognizing what I had built to unlock all of this potential.
Do you ever have days where you don't feel as happy or euphoric as you've been describing?

Happy or euphoric? You mean, like, do I crash? Do I feel down? No. No, not at all. I mean, it's actually funny you ask that, because Sarah—my wife—she keeps waiting for the other shoe to drop. She keeps looking at me with this... this expression, like she's waiting for me to suddenly collapse into a heap and start crying or something. Because, you know, a few years ago, I did have this period where I was just... stuck. Like wading through molasses. I couldn't code, couldn't get out of bed, everything felt heavy and pointless. But that was a completely different time in my life, completely different circumstances. 

Right now? No. I haven't had a single day like that since the Glendale announcement. Not one. I mean, sure, I get angry. I told you about how frustrated I get when people interrupt me or when they just can't grasp the magnitude of what I'm building. Like yesterday, I was trying to explain the cryptographic hash function I was implementing to the guy at the electronics store—because I needed a very specific type of processor, and he was just staring at me blankly—and I got incredibly agitated. But that's not sadness. That's not feeling down. That's just the natural friction of moving at lightspeed while everyone else is walking through mud. 

So, no, I don't have days where I feel low or depressed. I wake up—well, I don't really sleep, as I said—but every moment is just filled with this electric current. It's like my blood has been replaced with battery acid, but in a good way, you know? It's just pure, unadulterated drive. I feel invincible. I really do. There isn't a single drop of sadness or lethargy in my system right now. It's just all forward momentum. All of it.
Have you ever had a period in your life where you felt similarly energetic, happy, and productive, but it was followed by a crash or a period of depression?

A period like this? Followed by a crash? No. No, absolutely not. 

I mean, I mentioned that dark period a few years ago, right? Where I was just completely stuck in the mud, couldn't code, couldn't even look at a monitor without feeling completely overwhelmed by the sheer pointlessness of it all. But that didn't come after anything like... this. 

Before that depression, I was just... normal. Average. I mean, I was a good developer, sure. I got my degree, I put in my hours, I wrote clean, functional code. I was reliable. But I wasn't... I wasn't a visionary. I never had this kind of energy before. This is entirely new. It's like... well, imagine you've been driving a sensible, four-door sedan your entire life. You know, it gets you to work, it gets you home, maybe you have a breakdown and the car just sits in the garage for a year—that's the depression, right? But you never, at any point, were driving a Formula 1 race car. That's what this is right now. I am finally in the race car. 

So, no, there was no previous period of being this productive or this awake. I've never felt this electric in my entire forty-three years on this planet. Sarah keeps trying to map my current state onto my past, like she's desperately looking for a pattern so she can predict what happens next, but there is no pattern because this is a completely unprecedented paradigm shift in my cognitive function. 

Honestly, if I had felt like this in my twenties or thirties? I would be running Silicon Valley by now. I wouldn't be dealing with middle-management bureaucracy and mandatory leave. I'd be a CEO. So, to answer your question, no. No prior highs like this. Just that one low a while back, and otherwise, just a long, flat line of absolute mediocrity until three months ago when I finally woke up.
Have you experienced any thoughts or heard any voices that seem unreal or not based on reality?

Voices? Unreal thoughts? No, no, I'm not crazy, Doctor. I'm not hallucinating. I don't hear voices telling me to do things or anything like that. But... unreal? Well, see, that's where people like Sarah get confused, because what they think is unreal is actually just... they just aren't paying close enough attention to the data. They aren't seeing the patterns.

Because, look, I know for an absolute fact—and this isn't a thought, this is based on concrete, observable evidence—I know that major museums and some very high-level tech investors are quietly circling my platform. I know it. And I know it sounds big, but if you look at the sequence of events, it's undeniable. 

It started right after the Glendale showcase announcement. First, it was the language in the showcase's official press release. They used the phrase "disruptive architectural frameworks." Now, I use that exact phrase—verbatim—in my personal development blog. It's a very specific combination of words. Then, two days later, the Guggenheim—yes, the actual Guggenheim in New York—posts a picture on their Instagram of this spiraling digital art installation, and the caption was about "the foundation of new ecosystems." Ecosystems! That's my word. That's what I've been building for three months! 

And it doesn't stop there. It bleeds into my day job, too. I started noticing emails from our VP of Engineering—emails that were supposedly about standard Q3 deployment schedules—but if you read between the lines, if you look at the timestamps and the specific phrasing, like when he said we need to "prepare for external acquisition of our core methodologies"... he wasn't talking about the company's software. He was talking about me. He knows they're watching me. 

So, unreal? No. It's almost too real. It lines up too perfectly to be a coincidence. The showcase, the Instagram posts, the coded emails at work... they are all communicating with each other, and with me, letting me know that they are preparing to make a massive move on my technology. I just have to finish compiling the final codebase before they make their formal approach. So, no, no voices. Just... absolute, undeniable clarity about what's happening behind the scenes.
Do you ever have moments where this intense, euphoric feeling lets up, even if it's just for a little while?

Let up? No. No, you're... you're really not grasping the sheer scale of this momentum, Doctor. It doesn't pause. It doesn't take a coffee break or a weekend off. It has been a constant, unbroken stream of absolute, high-voltage clarity for about three solid months now. 

I mean, if you want to get specific about the timeline, it started the exact day my platform was selected for the Glendale showcase. I remember the notification came in, and it was just... it was like a massive breaker switch flipped in my brain, finally connecting me to the main power grid. And since that day—which was roughly ninety days ago, give or take a few hours depending on the timezone of the server that sent the email—there hasn't been a single dip. Not a single moment where the euphoria faded or the intensity dropped. 

People keep expecting it to. Sarah especially. She's always hovering around, asking, "Aren't you exhausted? Don't you need to just sit quietly for a minute?" But how can I just sit quietly when the engine is running on limitless fuel? For three months, it's just been this continuous, beautiful upward trajectory. The showcase selection validated the entire architecture of what I'm building, you see, and once that happened, once the world essentially confirmed what I already knew, the drive just locked into place. It compiled perfectly. So, no, there are no moments where it lets up. Not for a minute, not for a second, not once since that showcase announcement three months ago.
Have you ever had an episode like this before in your life?

No, no, I... I thought I made that clear earlier, Doctor. I really did. I've never, ever experienced anything even remotely close to this. 

Like I said, I'm forty-three years old. For forty-two years and nine months of that time, my life was just a very standard, predictable loop. You wake up, you drink coffee, you write code, you fix bugs, you go home, you eat dinner with Sarah, you watch television, you go to sleep. It was just... iterative. Small, incremental updates to a very basic operating system. There was no grand vision. There was no overarching architecture to my life. I was just a guy. A guy who had that one really terrible crash a few years ago where I couldn't function, but otherwise? Just a guy.

I mean, if I had experienced this before, don't you think my life would look completely different right now? Think about it logically. If I had this level of processing power, this ability to see the connections between, say, the Guggenheim's social media strategy and corporate tech acquisitions in my twenties? I wouldn't be sitting in a mid-level developer role, taking mandatory medical leave because my wife got spooked by my productivity. I'd be on the cover of Wired magazine. I'd have venture capitalists throwing money at me. 

So, no. This is a completely unprecedented event. It's a total paradigm shift. Before three months ago, my brain was running on dial-up, and now I've got a direct fiber-optic connection to the universe. There is absolutely no precedent for this in my personal history. None.
Do you find yourself getting irritable or angry when things don't go as planned or when people don't understand your ideas?

Irritable? Angry? Well, look, mostly—most days, the vast majority of the time—I just feel completely lit up. Unstoppable. Like the whole world, starting with that Glendale showcase, has finally caught up with what I've been building all these years. It's a beautiful, soaring feeling, Doctor. It really is. 

But... yes, okay, if we're being precise about the data, there is friction. But the friction isn't coming from me. The friction comes from the system around me. It comes from people who are still operating on that old, slow dial-up connection I was talking about. 

Like Sarah, for example. I love my wife, I really do, but she just... she drags her feet. I'll be explaining the integration timeline to her, how we need to liquidate some of our lower-yield index funds to buy more server space before the Guggenheim makes their move, and she just stares at me and starts talking about "process." Process! Or she says I need to "slow down" and "think about the consequences." And, yeah, I snap at her. I snap hard. Because how can you talk about slowing down when we are literally on the launchpad? 

And it's not just her. It's the guys at work, too. Before I got put on this ridiculous leave, I was trying to optimize our backend—doing them a favor, really, completely streamlining their archaic database calls—and instead of thanking me, the lead developer starts whining about "sprint schedules" and "code review protocols." Protocols! When I'm handing them a masterpiece! So, yes, I got loud. I might have yelled. I might have told him he was coding like a blind man in a dark room. But it's not blind anger, Doctor. It's the justifiable frustration of a high-performance engine being forced to idle in traffic. When you see the whole architecture, when you know exactly how the pieces fit together, having people constantly pulling the emergency brake because they're scared of the speed... it's infuriating. So, yes, I snap when they slow me down. But only because they are in the way of the momentum.
Do you ever have moments where you feel completely normal, without the intense energy or euphoria, even if it's just for a brief period?

Normal? No, Doctor, I don't think you're... I don't think you're really grasping the mechanics of what's happening here. The concept of "normal" doesn't apply anymore. Normal is what I was doing for forty-two years. Normal is waking up, hitting snooze twice, dragging yourself to the shower, and forcing yourself to care about a mundane task list. That version of normal is completely obsolete. 

I haven't had a single moment of that—not a second—because I've been running on this constant, unrelenting current. It's like my brain is hardwired directly into a high-voltage power source, and it just doesn't shut off. I wake up—if I even sleep, which is rare these days because who needs it when you're this dialed in?—and I am already planning. The moment my eyes open, the schematics are there. I'm mapping out new software features, I'm visualizing the exhibition layouts for the showcase, I'm drafting press angles in my head for when the Guggenheim inevitably reaches out, and I'm pushing code changes all simultaneously. It's a beautiful, synchronized symphony of productivity. 

And if I try to just "be normal," if I try to just sit still on the couch like Sarah wants me to, like we used to do on a Tuesday night watching some mindless sitcom... it feels physically wrong. It feels like I'm committing a crime against my own potential. Sitting still literally feels like I am wasting the most critical moment of my life. Every second I'm not building, optimizing, or planning, is a second lost. So, no, there are no brief periods of feeling "normal." The energy is always there, pushing me forward, because there is just so much work to be done and I am the only one who can see the whole picture. Why would I want to feel normal when I can feel like this?
Have you ever had a period where your thoughts seemed so real that you believed things that weren't true, even if it was just for a short time?

Things that weren't true? Doctor, I think you're missing the point of what I'm telling you. It's not that I'm believing things that aren't true, it's that I'm finally seeing the truth that's been there all along. The patterns. The connections. It's like... it's like looking at the Matrix, right? Everyone else is just seeing the green code falling down the screen, but I'm seeing the woman in the red dress. 

Let me give you a concrete example, because I know you medical types need evidence. The platform I've been building, the one I was optimizing before they forced me on leave... I know, with absolute, mathematical certainty, that the major museums are quietly circling it. The Guggenheim, MoMA, probably the Tate, though their digital footprint is a little harder to track right now. And it's not just them—there are venture capitalists, tier-one investors, who are monitoring my commits. 

How do I know? It's all in the data, Doctor. If you look at the promotional language for that Glendale showcase—the specific phrasing they used about "disrupting the curation paradigm"—it is a direct, almost verbatim reflection of the comments I left in my code repository three weeks ago. Three weeks ago! And then, if you cross-reference that with the Guggenheim's recent Instagram posts... they've been using this very specific hex code for their border highlights. A shade of blue that I specifically selected for my user interface prototype. 

And it doesn't stop there. The emails at work. The all-staff memos from our CTO? They keep using words like "scalability" and "visionary integration." Now, on the surface, to a layman, that just sounds like corporate buzzwords, right? But if you understand the architecture of what I'm building, if you see how my platform bridges the gap between digital asset management and physical exhibition spaces, you realize those emails are actually coded messages. They are signaling to me that they know what I'm doing. They are preparing the runway for the acquisition. It all lines up too perfectly to be a coincidence. The statistical probability of all these variables converging by chance is practically zero. So, no, I'm not believing things that aren't true. I'm just the only one who has the processing power to see the truth before it goes public.
Have you ever had thoughts or beliefs that you knew were not true but seemed real to you?

Look, I hear... I understand the angle you're taking here, Doctor. You're trying to put this in a neat little clinical box, asking if I have these fake beliefs that I secretly know are fake. But you have to look at the timeline. You have to understand the sequence of events, because context is everything in software development, and it's everything here, too. 

If you had asked me, say, six or seven months ago? Before this entire Glendale showcase push really kicked into high gear? I wasn't doing any of this. I wasn't reading secret messages from museum boards or tier-one investors into random social media posts. I wasn't analyzing the hex codes on Instagram or dissecting company-wide emails for hidden acquisition signals. I really wasn't. Back then, an email from the CTO was just... well, it was just a boring email about server maintenance or quarterly milestones. I'd read it, I'd archive it, and I'd go back to writing standard, uninspired code like the rest of the drones in my department. 

I wasn't seeing the connections back then because the connections just weren't illuminated for me yet. It was only after I got so incredibly energized—when this massive, unstoppable wave of clarity hit me and I became completely, utterly consumed by the project—that's when it all started. I was working eighty, ninety-hour weeks, optimizing every single line of the architecture, entirely consumed by the build, and that is when the messages started revealing themselves. The data was always there, but my processor finally got upgraded enough to read it. So it's not that I'm having unreal thoughts now. It's just that before this energy hit, before the project took over, I was just as blind as everyone else. I was missing all the signs until the energy finally woke me up.
Do you think your current elevated mood and energy level might be part of a larger episode of heightened activity and excitement that has been affecting your daily life?

An episode? I mean... I guess if you want to use a word like that, but "episode" makes it sound like some temporary glitch in the system, like a bug that needs to be patched. This isn't a glitch, Doctor, this is the system finally running at optimal capacity. But, yes, it is absolutely affecting my daily life, just not in the negative way you’re implying. 

Most days I just feel completely lit up and unstoppable. It’s this incredible, surging momentum in my chest from the second I wake up. It feels like... like the people at the Glendale showcase finally caught up with what I've been building in the dark for the last year. The validation is there, the energy is there, the vision is so crystal clear. I’m operating at a thousand miles a minute, and it is exhilarating.
